The Bornean grenadier anchovy Coilia borneensis is a small, pelagic fish species inhabiting coastal and estuarine waters of Southeast Asia. Field surveys indicate that this clupeiform reaches an ultimate total length of 12.4 cm [Li = 12.4 cm], a modest size that positions it among the smaller members of the Engraulidae family. Length-frequency distributions from gillnet samples suggest that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs when individuals reach a total length of 9.1 cm [Lp = 9.1 cm]. This size-based threshold is a common feature in indeterminate growers, where reproductive investment begins only after a substantial portion of somatic growth has been completed. The relatively narrow gap between these two length metrics implies a compressed period of adult growth following the onset of maturity, consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early and repeated reproductive bouts over prolonged somatic expansion in a variable inshore environment.

Reproduction in this species is characterized by a pelagic egg phase, with fertilized ova drifting in the water column until eclosion. Observations under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] reveal that the age at birth, marking the moment of chorion rupture and emergence of the yolk-sac larva, is 5 days [ab = 5 days]. This rapid developmental pace is typical of tropical anchovies, where elevated water temperatures accelerate embryogenesis and shorten the incubation window. The newly hatched larva carries a substantial yolk reserve, enabling an endotrophic phase before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding begins. The wet weight at birth, calculated from the egg diameter of 0.6 mm, is 0.00011 grams [Wwb = 0.00011 grams], an extremely low mass that underscores the minute size of the prolarvae at the onset of their free-swimming life.

As the yolk-sac larva transitions to exogenous feeding, it enters a period of rapid somatic growth that continues through the pelagic larval phase and juvenile stage. The species exhibits a clear length-weight relationship derived from large sample collections, described by the allometric equation W = 0.00282 * L^3.10. From this relationship, the ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum body mass attained by fully grown adults, is estimated at 6.91 grams [Wwi = 6.91 grams]. In parallel, the wet weight at puberty, or the mass at which gonadal recrudescence begins, is 2.65 grams [Wwp = 2.65 grams]. This approximately 2.6-fold mass increase from puberty to the asymptotic weight reflects the substantial energetic resources allocated to somatic growth and lipid storage that continue even after reproductive capability is attained, a pattern common in iteroparous pelagic spawners.

Longevity records for Coilia borneensis were assessed through otolith-based age estimation on a sample of individuals maintained under constant temperature conditions. The maximum lifespan observed under these controlled conditions, at a rearing temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], was 730 days [am = 730 days]. This lifespan, equivalent to two years, is relatively brief compared to many temperate anchovy species but is consistent with the accelerated metabolic and reproductive schedules typical of small tropical fishes. The synchronous control of developmental events by water temperature is evident when comparing the 5-day incubation period (5 days) [ab = 5 days] at the same thermal regime, highlighting how a single environmental variable governs both early ontogeny and total lifespan duration in this ectothermic species at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

Ecologically, the short two-year lifespan (2 years) [am = 2 years] and early maturation at 9.1 cm [Lp = 9.1 cm] total length position Coilia borneensis as a species with a high turnover rate, likely adapted to the seasonal productivity pulses of Bornean coastal ecosystems at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Adult body length stabilizes at 12.4 cm [Li = 12.4 cm], a value consistent with the species' trophic position as a planktivore. The maximum body mass of mature adults reaches 6.91 grams [Wwi = 6.91 grams], reflecting the species' small size relative to other engraulids. The body mass at which gonadal recrudescence begins is 2.65 grams [Wwp = 2.65 grams], a value typical for engraulids of comparable adult size, representing a proportion of ultimate length that balances early fecundity with the energetic demands of continued growth in a resource-limited estuary.
